adapt_rules.txt:
General SNACS adaptation notes from reviewed guidelines/examples:

1) Motion verb + to + institution/place can take a nonlocative scene role reflecting the semantic type of the landmark, while function remains Goal. Example: "Went to the school" -> role p.Org, function p.Goal.

2) Partitive each/one/all/some/plenty/etc. + of + NP:
   - canonical partition/member reading: role p.QuantityItem, function p.Whole. Examples: "Each of you", "one of them".
   - amount noun measuring a set may also be annotated role=function p.QuantityItem. Example: "plenty of options".

3) Adjectives of emotion/evaluation with of/with marking what the feeling or judgment concerns often take Stimulus~Topic. Examples: "proud of your massive contributions", "pleased with that one".

4) Possessive pronouns/genitives are highly construction-sensitive:
   - creator/actor/holder of a nominalized action or support noun can be role p.Agent, function p.Gestalt. Examples: "your massive contributions", "her help".
   - ordinary ownership/association with a concrete possessed item: p.Possessor~p.Possessor. Example: "your money", "my dogs".
   - kin/professional/social relation readings can be scene role p.SocialRel with function p.Gestalt. Example: "my PA".
   - part-whole/body-part possession often uses role p.Whole, function p.Gestalt. Examples: "my hair", "car's gears".
   - beneficiary-oriented genitives may surface with function p.Possessor but scene role p.Beneficiary. Example: "the bus boys' station".

5) Temporal span expressions with throughout mark p.Duration~p.Duration. Example: "throughout the year".

6) by + gerund indicating the method used to perform a communicative/action predicate is p.Means~p.Means. Example: "start out by saying".

7) Business names, roads, and highways with at/on used literally for location are p.Locus~p.Locus. Examples: "at Lovely Nails", "on Military Road", "on highway".

8) to + infinitive expressing intended result/function is p.Purpose~p.Purpose. Examples: "to get napkins", "made to suit me".

9) Predicate adjective with to-marked affected person can show scene/function mismatch; e.g. "important to them" -> p.Experiencer~p.Goal.

10) like:
   - straightforward comparison standard: p.ComparisonRef~p.ComparisonRef. Example: "like driving a new car".
   - identity/typing via resemblance wording can be p.Identity~p.ComparisonRef. Example: "a heart surgeon like him".

11) for may mark pure Beneficiary or Purpose; in evaluative scalar expressions it can be ComparisonRef~Purpose. Examples: "do nothing for you" (Beneficiary~Beneficiary), "much for daycare" (ComparisonRef~Purpose), "things for earrings" (Purpose~Purpose).

12) Lexicalized expressions:
   - far from X -> p.Source~p.Source.
   - at least -> p.Extent~p.Extent.
   - all over -> p.Locus~p.Locus.

13) of after support/identity nouns may be p.Identity~p.Identity. Example: "a great job of taking care...".

Useful caution:
- Do not overgeneralize possessives to p.Possessor; event nominals often license participant roles (Agent, Theme, Beneficiary, SocialRel, Whole, etc.) with function p.Gestalt or, in special constructions, p.Possessor.
- Role may reflect the scene relation while function reflects the lexical contribution of the adposition/case marker; e.g., destination marker 'to' still contributes Goal even when landmark role is p.Org, and adjective-selected 'to' may contribute Goal while the scene role is p.Experiencer.
- For partitives, distinguish partition/member readings (QuantityItem~Whole) from measure/amount uses like "plenty of options" (QuantityItem~QuantityItem).
